source: FAO Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, "Swine Health Management, Volume 3: Frequently Asked Questions on Pig Biosecurity and Disease Reporting", RAP Publication 2012/27, Bangkok, 2012. Acknowledgements credit national focal points from Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Philippines, Thailand and Viet Nam as contributors.
text: Reasons and practical guidance for reporting suspected animal disease: reporting quickly helps protect not just one farmer's own herd but neighboring farms, since it allows authorities to warn others and act before disease spreads further, and it supports the long-term health and marketability of the national pig herd. Situations that should be reported immediately include: an unusual increase in the number of sick or dead pigs; pigs showing unusual or severe clinical signs; and pigs that continue to show disease signs even though they were vaccinated. Reports should go to the local (commune/district/provincial) agriculture or veterinary office, or to national animal health authorities, as soon as unusual signs are noticed - not after waiting to see if the problem resolves on its own.
